records.name: Frederick Douglass
records.scaleNote: A defining figure: three autobiographies (1845, 1855, 1881), decades of speeches and newspapers, and a National Historic Site; his Wye House childhood is documented in his own Narrative.
records.origins: Born enslaved in February 1818 in Talbot County on Maryland's Eastern Shore, the son of Harriet Bailey and an unnamed white man. His owner, Aaron Anthony, was clerk and chief overseer for Colonel Edward Lloyd V, and as a small child Douglass lived on Lloyd's home plantation, Wye House.
records.role_summary: Sent to Baltimore at about eight, he learned to read in Hugh Auld's household and later worked in the Fells Point shipyards; returned to the Eastern Shore, he was hired out to the 'slave-breaker' Edward Covey and fought back. On 3 September 1838 he escaped by train and ferry dressed as a sailor, with help from Anna Murray, reaching New York in under a day, and became the most influential Black abolitionist, editor and orator of the century.

roleDetail.d: His Narrative describes the Lloyd estate's 'Great House Farm', the whipping of his aunt Hester and the hunger of enslaved children; scholars place him there c. 1824–1826.
Sophia Auld began teaching him the alphabet until her husband forbade it; Douglass kept learning from street boys and bought The Columbian Orator at about twelve.

After escaping in 1838 he settled in New Bedford, lectured for the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, published his Narrative (1845) and founded The North Star (1847); British supporters bought his legal freedom in 1846.
He recruited Black soldiers in the Civil War, became US Marshal for DC (1877), Recorder of Deeds (1881) and US Minister to Haiti (1889–1891).

records.legacy: Cedar Hill, his Anacostia home, is the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site. Descendants, including Kenneth B. Morris Jr. (also a descendant of Booker T. Washington), run Frederick Douglass Family Initiatives against modern slavery. Bronze statues of Douglass and Harriet Tubman were installed in the Maryland State House's Old House of Delegates chamber in 2020.

legacyDetail.d: Frederick Douglass Family Initiatives, founded 2007 in Rochester, NY, works on anti-trafficking education and its 'One Million Abolitionists' book project.

Douglass revisited the Eastern Shore in 1877–1881, meeting his former owner Thomas Auld and visiting Wye House; the Lloyd estate is still in the family and archaeology there has used his descriptions.

sources.label: Docsouth (UNC) — Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845)
AAIHS — The Legacy of Frederick Douglass: an interview with Kenneth B. Morris Jr.

connections.label: enslaved as a child on Edward Lloyd V's estate
fellow Eastern Shore abolitionist; 1868 tribute letter
Cedar Hill home preserved by NPS

records.name: Harriet Tubman
records.scaleNote: Documented by Sarah Bradford's 1869/1886 biographies, Maryland court and estate records, Civil War pension files and modern biographies (Kate Clifford Larson, 2004); a National Historical Park bears her name.
records.origins: Born Araminta Ross around 1822 in Dorchester County on Maryland's Eastern Shore, enslaved by the Brodess family; several of her sisters were sold away. As a teenager she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a weight at another enslaved person.
records.role_summary: Fearing sale after her owner's death, she escaped alone to Philadelphia in 1849, then returned repeatedly to the Eastern Shore to lead out family and others. In the Civil War she worked as a nurse, scout and spy for the Union and guided the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina on 2 June 1863, which freed about 750 people.

roleDetail.d: Larson's archival research documents about 13 trips back to Maryland bringing out roughly 70 people, mostly family and friends, and instructions to some 50–60 others who escaped on their own; the older claim of '300 people in 19 trips' (Bradford) is an exaggeration.
Per the NPS she was the only woman to lead an armed military operation in the war, guiding Union gunboats and Black troops up the Combahee; c. 750 people were freed.
She settled in Auburn, NY, fought for a war pension, supported women's suffrage and opened a home for elderly African Americans before dying in 1913.

records.legacy: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park and the Maryland state park visitor centre interpret her Dorchester County landscape. A Tubman statue joined Douglass in the Maryland State House in 2020, and a Treasury redesign of the $20 note featuring her has been announced and delayed more than once.

legacyDetail.d: A national monument was proclaimed in Maryland in 2013 and national historical parks were established in Maryland and Auburn, NY, in 2014.

sources.label: NPS — Maryland: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park
Maryland State Archives — Harriet Ross Tubman Davis (MSA SC 5496-13562)
National Trust for Historic Preservation — Interview: Kate Clifford Larson on Harriet Tubman

connections.label: Maryland abolished slavery during the war she fought in
brought her niece's family out via Baltimore (1850)

records.name: Josiah Henson
records.scaleNote: His 1849 narrative (expanded 1858, 1876–81), Canadian records and the Riley farm site document his life; Harriet Beecher Stowe cited him as a source for Uncle Tom's Cabin.
records.base: Isaac Riley farm, North Bethesda, Montgomery County, Maryland
records.origins: Born enslaved in 1789 in Charles County, Maryland; as a child he saw his family sold apart at an estate sale. He was bought by Isaac Riley and grew up on Riley's farm in Montgomery County, becoming its overseer and a Methodist preacher.
records.role_summary: Sent by Riley to walk other enslaved people to Kentucky, he declined a chance to free them in Ohio, later saying he regretted it. After being cheated out of a purchase of his own freedom and taken to New Orleans to be sold — a sale averted only when his owner's nephew fell ill — he escaped with his wife and children in 1830, reaching Upper Canada on 28 October 1830 via the Underground Railroad.

roleDetail.d: Near Dresden, Ontario, he helped found the Dawn community and the British-American Institute, a school for formerly enslaved people.
By his own account he went back into the US to help about 118 people escape.
Stowe's Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1853) named him as a model; the novel's passive character distorts Henson, who actively resisted.

records.legacy: The Josiah Henson Museum and Park, on the surviving Riley farmhouse in North Bethesda, is run by Montgomery Parks and opened as a museum in 2021. In Dresden, Ontario, his home is the Josiah Henson Museum of African-Canadian History (formerly 'Uncle Tom's Cabin Historic Site').

legacyDetail.d: Montgomery County parks bought the Riley/Bolten House in 2006; it is on the National Register of Historic Places.

sources.label: Montgomery Parks — Josiah Henson Museum & Park
Docsouth (UNC) — The Life of Josiah Henson (1849)
Dictionary of Canadian Biography — Henson, Josiah

connections.label: escaped to Canada 1830; later guided others

records.name: Benjamin Banneker
records.scaleNote: Documented by his almanacs (1792–1797), his surviving journal, the 1791 Banneker–Jefferson correspondence and the federal district survey records.
records.base: Ellicott's Lower Mills (Oella), Baltimore County, Maryland
records.origins: Born free in 1731 in Baltimore County to Mary Banneky, a free woman, and Robert, a formerly enslaved African; tradition holds his grandmother Molly Welsh was an English indentured servant who married an African man she had bought and freed. He farmed tobacco on the family's land and taught himself mathematics and astronomy.
records.role_summary: He built a wooden striking clock as a young man and, with instruments lent by the Quaker Ellicott family, taught himself astronomy. In 1791 he assisted Andrew Ellicott on the survey of the new federal district, then published almanacs that abolitionists promoted as proof of Black intellectual equality.

roleDetail.d: On 19 August 1791 he sent Thomas Jefferson his almanac manuscript and a letter attacking the hypocrisy of slavery under the Declaration's principles; Jefferson replied on 30 August.
He worked for about three months in 1791 on Ellicott's survey of the boundaries of the District of Columbia.
His almanacs were published from 1792 to 1797 in Baltimore and other cities, the 1793 edition reprinting the Jefferson exchange.

records.legacy: The Benjamin Banneker Historical Park and Museum in Oella (Baltimore County) stands on his farm site with a replica cabin; most of his possessions were destroyed when his house burned on the day of his funeral in 1806. Schools, a DC park and a US postage stamp (1980) honour him.

legacyDetail.d: Popular claims that he redrew L'Enfant's plan of Washington from memory are not supported by evidence.

sources.label: Founders Online — To Thomas Jefferson from Benjamin Banneker, 19 August 1791
Encyclopedia Virginia — Letter from Benjamin Banneker to Thomas Jefferson (1791)

connections.label: surveyed the federal district Washington selected (1791)

records.name: The Georgetown 272 (GU272)
records.scaleNote: Documented by the 1838 bill of sale and Jesuit records in the Georgetown Slavery Archive; the Georgetown Memory Project has identified 200+ of those sold and thousands of living descendants.
records.lifespan: Enslaved on Maryland Jesuit plantations c. 1717–1838; in Louisiana 1838–1865
records.base: Jesuit plantations of southern Maryland (White Marsh, St. Inigoes, Newtown, St. Thomas Manor)
records.origins: The Maryland Province of the Society of Jesus held enslaved families for over a century on plantations in Prince George's, St. Mary's and Charles counties, whose income supported Jesuit institutions including Georgetown College. Many of the families had been Catholic for generations.
records.role_summary: In 1838 Jesuit leaders Thomas Mulledy and William McSherry sold 272 men, women and children to Louisiana planters Henry Johnson and Jesse Batey for about $115,000, partly to pay Georgetown's debts. Families were shipped from Alexandria to New Orleans and forced to work sugar and cotton plantations in Ascension, Iberville and Terrebonne parishes; some escaped being sent.

roleDetail.d: Isaac Hawkins, 65, is the first person named in the 1838 articles of agreement; Georgetown renamed a building Isaac Hawkins Hall in 2017.
Sold as a boy of about 13, he was taken to Maringouin, Louisiana, where his gravestone survives; his descendant, journalist Maxine Crump, learned of him through the Georgetown Memory Project in 2016.
Georgetown's 2016 working group found that part of the proceeds paid off the college's debts; the sale was opposed by some Jesuits at the time.

records.legacy: Georgetown apologised in 2017, renamed two buildings, offers admissions preference to descendants and created a Reconciliation Fund after a 2019 student referendum. In 2021 the Jesuits pledged $100m toward the Descendants Truth & Reconciliation Foundation, with a $1bn goal. Descendants organise through the GU272 Descendants Association and research ancestry via the American Ancestors GU272 database.

legacyDetail.d: In Maringouin, Louisiana, many residents descend from those sold in 1838.
American Ancestors (NEHGS) and the Georgetown Memory Project maintain searchable GU272 family trees.

sources.label: Georgetown University — Isaac Hawkins Hall renaming
American Ancestors — How to Find Your GU272 Ancestor

connections.label: sold in 1838 to pay college debts

records.name: Daniel Coker
records.scaleNote: Documented by his 1810 Dialogue Between a Virginian and an African Minister, AME records and his published 1820 Journal of the voyage to Africa.
records.origins: Born Isaac Wright in Frederick County, Maryland, to an enslaved father and an English indentured mother; he escaped to New York, became a Methodist preacher, and returned to Baltimore under a new name, where his freedom was later purchased.
records.role_summary: He taught at the African school of Baltimore's Sharp Street church and led Black Methodists out of white-controlled churches to form Bethel in Baltimore. At the 1816 Philadelphia convention founding the AME Church he was elected its first bishop but stepped aside for Richard Allen. In 1820 he sailed on the Elizabeth with the first American Colonization Society emigrants and stayed in Sierra Leone as a missionary and colonial administrator.

roleDetail.d: His 1810 Dialogue Between a Virginian and an African Minister is one of the earliest anti-slavery pamphlets by an African American.
Elected bishop at the 1816 AME convention, he declined or resigned the next day; reasons are disputed.
After the deadly Sherbro landing in 1820 he settled at Hastings near Freetown, where he died in 1846.

records.legacy: Bethel AME Church in Baltimore traces its founding to Coker's congregation. He is remembered in both AME and Sierra Leonean church history.

legacyDetail.d: Bethel AME, now on Druid Hill Avenue, is one of the oldest Black congregations in Maryland.

sources.label: Historical Society of Pennsylvania — Daniel Coker, 1780–1846

connections.label: fellow promoter of emigration to Sierra Leone

records.name: Henry Highland Garnet
records.scaleNote: Documented by his speeches (the 1843 Address to the Slaves; the 1865 Memorial Discourse), James McCune Smith's 1865 biography and convention records.
records.origins: Born enslaved in 1815 in Kent County on Maryland's Eastern Shore. In 1824 his family obtained permission to attend a funeral and instead escaped north, settling in New York City, where he attended the African Free School.
records.role_summary: A Presbyterian minister, he called in 1843 at the National Negro Convention in Buffalo for enslaved people to resist their enslavers ('Let your motto be resistance!'), a speech Frederick Douglass and others then opposed as too radical. On 12 February 1865 he became the first African American to preach in the US Capitol, in the House chamber.

roleDetail.d: The convention narrowly declined to endorse the speech; it was published in 1848 with David Walker's Appeal.
He supported the African Civilization Society and was appointed US Minister to Liberia in 1881, dying there in 1882.

records.legacy: Garnet is commemorated in Kent County, Maryland, and his 1865 sermon was reissued in 2020 as 'Let the Monster Perish'. Schools in Maryland and New York bear his name.

legacyDetail.d: His House sermon came days after Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment.

sources.label: Common Sense for the Eastern Shore — 'Let the Monster Perish!' Garnet's 1865 address

connections.label: New York Black press and activist circle

records.name: Hemings family (Elizabeth and Sally Hemings)
records.scaleNote: Documented in Jefferson's Farm Book and memoranda, Madison Hemings's 1873 recollections, the 1998 Y-DNA study and the Thomas Jefferson Foundation's 2000 report; Getting Word has interviewed 200+ Monticello descendants.
records.origins: Elizabeth Hemings, the daughter of an African woman and an English sea captain, was enslaved by John Wayles, with whom she had six children including Sally; that made Sally the half-sister of Jefferson's wife Martha Wayles. The family came to Jefferson through the Wayles inheritance in 1774.
records.role_summary: Sally Hemings accompanied Jefferson's daughter to Paris in 1787, where she could have claimed freedom; by Madison Hemings's account she returned in 1789 after Jefferson promised to free their children. She had at least six children, four of whom survived — Beverly, Harriet, Madison and Eston — all of whom left slavery: two allowed to leave in 1822, two freed by Jefferson's will in 1826. Her brother James, trained as a chef in Paris, negotiated his freedom in 1796.

roleDetail.d: Sally Hemings was never formally emancipated; after 1826 Jefferson's daughter Martha Randolph gave her 'her time' and she lived with her sons in Charlottesville until 1835.
A 1998 DNA study linked Eston Hemings's male-line descendants to the Jefferson male line; the Foundation concluded in 2000 that Jefferson very likely fathered Eston and probably all six children.
She was about 14–16 when the relationship began; historians stress she was enslaved and could not freely consent.

records.legacy: Monticello opened 'The Life of Sally Hemings' exhibit in 2018 in a room tradition associates with her, and its Getting Word oral-history project (since 1993) records Hemings and other descendant families, some of whom attend Monticello reunions. Descendants of Madison and Eston carry family histories through up to eight generations.

legacyDetail.d: Most Getting Word interviewees trace descent to Elizabeth Hemings.
Monticello's signage and tours now state that Jefferson fathered Hemings's children.

sources.label: Monticello — The Life of Sally Hemings

connections.label: enslaved by Jefferson; Sally bore his children
Paris 1787–89, where slavery had no legal basis

records.name: Ona Judge
records.scaleNote: Documented by Washington's correspondence and runaway advertisements, plus her own interviews in the Granite Freeman (1845) and The Liberator (1847); Erica Armstrong Dunbar's Never Caught (2017).
records.base: Mount Vernon, Virginia; later Greenland, New Hampshire
records.origins: Born at Mount Vernon around 1773 to Betty, an enslaved seamstress, and Andrew Judge, an English indentured tailor. As a 'dower' slave of the Custis estate she belonged to Martha Washington's first husband's heirs, not to Washington himself.
records.role_summary: A personal attendant to Martha Washington at the President's House in Philadelphia, she fled on 21 May 1796 after learning she was to be given to Martha's granddaughter Eliza Custis. Free Black Philadelphians helped her board a ship to Portsmouth, New Hampshire; Washington twice tried to recover her through agents, but she refused to return and lived free, though legally a fugitive, until her death in 1848.

roleDetail.d: The Washingtons rotated enslaved household workers out of Pennsylvania to avoid its 1780 gradual abolition law's six-month residency rule.
Washington's agent Joseph Whipple met her in 1796 and his nephew Burwell Bassett tried again in 1799; Senator John Langdon reportedly warned her.

records.legacy: Her story is told at Mount Vernon and the President's House site in Philadelphia, and in Dunbar's Never Caught. She married sailor Jack Staines in 1797; her children predeceased her.

legacyDetail.d: Her 1840s interviews are rare first-person testimony from someone enslaved by a US president.

sources.label: House Divided (Dickinson College) — Ona Judge defies President George Washington

connections.label: fellow member of Washington's enslaved household

records.name: William Lee
records.scaleNote: Documented by Washington's purchase records (1768), wartime accounts, John Trumbull's 1780 portrait and Washington's 1799 will.
records.origins: Bought by George Washington in 1768, along with his brother Frank, from the estate of Mary Lee of Westmoreland County. He became Washington's personal valet and huntsman.
records.role_summary: Lee was at Washington's side throughout the Revolutionary War, from Cambridge to Yorktown, and appears beside him in Trumbull's portrait. Knee injuries later disabled him; in his 1799 will Washington freed him immediately — the only person so freed — with a $30 annual annuity, citing his 'faithful services during the Revolutionary War'. He remained at Mount Vernon as a shoemaker.

roleDetail.d: The other people Washington held were to be freed after Martha's death; the 150+ 'dower' people of the Custis estate were not his to free.
Lee asked Washington in 1784 to bring his wife Margaret Thomas, a free Black woman from Philadelphia, to Mount Vernon.

records.legacy: Mount Vernon interprets his life in its slavery exhibitions and at the Slave Memorial and burial ground (memorial dedicated 1983).

legacyDetail.d: Sources give 1810, 1811 or 1828.

connections.label: lived and died at Mount Vernon
Custis dower people excluded from Washington's will

records.name: Nat Turner
records.scaleNote: The deadliest US slave revolt; documented by trial records, Thomas R. Gray's The Confessions of Nat Turner (1831) and Virginia legislative debates.
records.origins: Born enslaved in Southampton County in 1800, he learned to read, became a lay preacher known for visions, and was sold or passed between several local owners, separated from his wife.
records.role_summary: On the night of 21–22 August 1831 he led a band that grew to some 60–70 people from farm to farm, killing about 55 white people, before militia defeated them near Jerusalem (now Courtland). Turner hid for two months; captured on 30 October, he was hanged on 11 November 1831. Trials condemned dozens; vigilantes and militia killed scores of Black people, many uninvolved.

roleDetail.d: Per Encyclopedia Virginia, 30 enslaved people and one free Black man were condemned; 19 were executed and others transported.
Gray's pamphlet is the main source for Turner's words; historians debate how much reflects Gray.
Virginia debated gradual emancipation in 1831–32 and rejected it; it and other states then tightened laws on Black literacy, preaching and assembly.

records.legacy: Turner's Bible is displayed at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. His revolt remains contested in memory, from William Styron's 1967 novel to the 2016 film The Birth of a Nation.

legacyDetail.d: A state historical marker in Southampton County notes the revolt; there is no monument to the rebels.

sources.label: Library of Virginia — 'To Be Hung by the Neck': Nat Turner

records.name: Gabriel (Gabriel's Conspiracy)
records.scaleNote: Documented by Henrico County court records, Governor James Monroe's correspondence and trial testimony.
records.base: Brookfield plantation, Henrico County (near Richmond), Virginia
records.origins: Born enslaved in 1776 on Thomas Prosser's Brookfield tobacco plantation outside Richmond; he became a literate, skilled blacksmith often hired out in the city. In 1799 he was branded for fighting a white man, escaping hanging only through 'benefit of clergy'.
records.role_summary: In 1800 he organised enslaved and some free workers around Richmond to seize the capitol and armoury, take Governor Monroe hostage and demand freedom, invoking revolutionary ideals. A storm on 30 August delayed the rising and two enslaved men, Tom and Pharoah, betrayed it; Gabriel fled by schooner to Norfolk but was caught and hanged on 10 October 1800, one of 26 executed.

roleDetail.d: Testimony suggests the rebels drew on the American and Haitian revolutions and sought allies among poor whites.
In 2007 Governor Tim Kaine issued an informal pardon for Gabriel and those executed with him.

records.legacy: Richmond has a historical marker and Gabriel is commemorated on the Richmond Slave Trail; the 2007 pardon was symbolic.

legacyDetail.d: The plot led Virginia in 1806 to require newly freed people to leave the state within a year.

sources.label: Founders Online — James T. Callender to Jefferson, 1800

connections.label: reported to Jefferson during the 1800 election
Haitian Revolution inspired and alarmed Virginians

records.name: Angela and the Africans of 1619
records.scaleNote: Known from John Rolfe's 1619 letter ('20. and odd Negroes'), the 1624/25 Virginia muster and Spanish/Portuguese shipping records; Angela appears only as a name in the muster.
records.lifespan: Captured c. 1618–1619; Angela recorded at Jamestown 1625
records.base: Point Comfort (Fort Monroe) and Jamestown, Virginia
records.origins: They were Kimbundu-speaking people of the Kingdom of Ndongo, captured during Portuguese Angola's 1618–1620 wars (with Imbangala allies) against Ndongo and shipped from Luanda on the São João Bautista toward Veracruz.
records.role_summary: English privateers White Lion and Treasurer attacked the Portuguese ship in the Gulf of Mexico and took about 60 captives. In late August 1619 the White Lion traded '20 and odd' of them at Point Comfort for food; days later the Treasurer arrived and left a few, including Angela, who by 1625 lived in the Jamestown household of Captain William Peirce.

roleDetail.d: Whether the first Africans were treated as lifelong slaves or as servants who could become free varied; Virginia law made slavery hereditary only from 1662.
Names like Angela and Antonio suggest some had been baptised in Angola by the Portuguese.
Jamestown Rediscovery has excavated the 'Angela Site' on the Peirce property.

records.legacy: Fort Monroe National Monument (2011) marks the landing; the 2019 commemoration of 400 years ('1619') was national, and an African Landing Memorial is being built at Fort Monroe.

legacyDetail.d: The date has become a focus of national debate, including the 2019 '1619 Project'; historians note Africans were in Spanish Florida earlier.

sources.label: NPS — Arrival of the First Africans in 1619
Fort Monroe Authority — 1619 African Landing Memorial

connections.label: captured in the wars against Ndongo
shipped from Luanda on the São João Bautista
Imbangala allies of the Portuguese took captives

records.name: Anthony Johnson
records.scaleNote: Documented in Virginia muster and Northampton County court records, including the 1655 Johnson v. Casor ruling; often cited, sometimes misleadingly, as 'the first slaveowner'.
records.base: Pungoteague Creek, Northampton County, Virginia; later Somerset County, Maryland
records.origins: Brought to Virginia in 1621 as 'Antonio a Negro', probably originally from Angola, he worked on the Bennett plantation, survived the 1622 Powhatan attack, married a woman named Mary, and by about the 1640s had gained his freedom.
records.role_summary: By 1651 he held about 250 acres on the Eastern Shore, partly through headrights. In 1653–1655 John Casor, a Black man in his service, claimed his indenture had expired; the Northampton court ruled in March 1655 that Casor belonged to Johnson for life. The Johnsons moved to Somerset County, Maryland, in the 1660s, where he died about 1670.

roleDetail.d: Johnson v. Casor (1655) is often described as the first civil case in the English colonies to hold a person who had committed no crime in lifelong servitude (John Punch had been sentenced to life servitude as a punishment in 1640). It was not the legal origin of slavery in Virginia, and white planters held far more people.
In 1670 a Virginia jury ruled his land could escheat because he was 'a Negroe and by consequence an alien'.
His grandson John Johnson named his Maryland farm 'Angola'.

records.legacy: His story shows that free Black property-holding was possible in early Virginia before laws hardened race-based slavery. It is frequently misused online to downplay white slaveholding; mainstream historians treat it as an exception within a closing window.

legacyDetail.d: Claims that Johnson was 'the first slaveowner in America' are wrong: Africans were enslaved in Spanish and Portuguese America a century earlier, and in Virginia people were held in lifelong bondage before 1655; laws made slavery hereditary and racial from 1662.

sources.label: Facing History & Ourselves — Anthony Johnson: A Man in Control of His Own Life

connections.label: moved to Maryland as lifelong slavery became law

records.name: Denmark Vesey
records.scaleNote: Known from the 1822 Charleston court proceedings and official accounts; historian Michael P. Johnson (2001) argued the plot was largely constructed by the court, a view other historians dispute.
records.origins: Enslaved as a boy in the Caribbean (probably St Thomas), he was bought by Charleston slave-ship captain Joseph Vesey. In 1799 he won a city lottery prize and in 1800 bought his freedom, working as a carpenter.
records.role_summary: A leader in Charleston's African Methodist congregation (forerunner of Mother Emanuel AME), he was accused in 1822 of planning a rising of enslaved people to seize the city and possibly sail for Haiti. Betrayed before it began, he and dozens of others were tried by a special court; 35 were hanged, including Vesey, and dozens more deported.

roleDetail.d: Michael P. Johnson (William and Mary Quarterly, 2001) argued that frightened officials and the court largely constructed the conspiracy from coerced testimony; Douglas Egerton, Robert Paquette and others reply that a real plan existed. The scale of the plot remains debated.
Authorities closed the African church, which was destroyed; the congregation met in secret until 1865.

records.legacy: A Vesey monument was unveiled in Charleston's Hampton Park in 2014. Mother Emanuel AME, which traces its roots to his congregation, was the site of the 2015 racist massacre of nine worshippers.

legacyDetail.d: The International African American Museum (2023) interprets Charleston's slavery history, including Vesey.

connections.label: reportedly hoped for refuge in Haiti

records.name: William Ellison
records.scaleNote: Per Johnson & Roark's Black Masters (1984) and the South Carolina Encyclopedia, he held 63 enslaved people in 1860, the most of any free Black person in South Carolina.
records.origins: Born enslaved as April around 1790 in South Carolina, possibly the son of his owner, he was apprenticed to cotton-gin maker William McCreight. He bought his own freedom in 1816 and changed his name to William.
records.role_summary: Ellison built a successful cotton-gin business at Stateburg, then bought land and enslaved people, becoming a cotton planter with about 900 acres and 63 enslaved people by 1860. He bought freedom for his wife and children but not for others he held; at the start of the Civil War his family supported the Confederacy.

roleDetail.d: Black slaveholders were few; many held only family members to protect them, but Ellison held people for profit like his white neighbours.
The family held a pew on the main floor of Stateburg's Holy Cross Episcopal Church, a marker of status.

records.legacy: His story, reconstructed from family letters found in his house, is studied as an example of how free people of colour navigated a slave society. It is sometimes misused to minimise slavery; historians stress how exceptional he was.

legacyDetail.d: Michael P. Johnson and James L. Roark's Black Masters (1984) is the main study, based on the Ellison family papers.

sources.label: South Carolina Public Radio — E is for Ellison, William (ca. 1790–1861)

connections.label: free Black slaveholder in an earlier era

records.name: Paul Cuffe
records.scaleNote: Documented by his ships' papers, letters, the 1780 Dartmouth tax petition and the 1815 Traveller manifest (National Archives).
records.origins: Born free on Cuttyhunk Island in 1759 to Kofi (Cuffe Slocum), an Akan man from West Africa who had been enslaved and freed, and Ruth Moses, a Wampanoag woman. He went to sea as a teenager.
records.role_summary: In 1780 he and his brother petitioned Massachusetts against taxation of Black men who could not vote. He built a fleet and a fortune in coastal and Atlantic trade with largely Black and Native crews. Hoping to link African Americans with Sierra Leone, he sailed there in 1811 and in 1815 carried 38 Black emigrants on his brig Traveller, largely at his own expense.

roleDetail.d: When customs seized the Traveller in 1812, he went to Washington and Madison ordered it released.
A Quaker, he built a racially integrated school in Westport.

records.legacy: He is commemorated in Westport, Massachusetts, by the Paul Cuffe Heritage project and a memorial at the Westport Friends Meeting House, where he is buried.

legacyDetail.d: His Sierra Leone scheme preceded the American Colonization Society, which many Black Americans later opposed.

records.name: James Forten
records.scaleNote: Documented by his business records, the 1813 Letters from a Man of Colour, convention minutes and Julie Winch's biography A Gentleman of Color (2002).
records.origins: Born free in Philadelphia in 1766, he attended Anthony Benezet's Quaker school. At about 14 he served as a powder boy on the privateer Royal Louis and spent months on the British prison ship Jersey.
records.role_summary: He took over sailmaker Robert Bridges's loft in 1798 and became one of the wealthiest Black Americans, employing Black and white workers. He fought Pennsylvania laws to restrict Black migration, led opposition to the American Colonization Society from 1817 and largely financed William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator in 1831.

roleDetail.t: Letters from a Man of Colour (1813).
roleDetail.d: His pamphlet attacked a proposed Pennsylvania bill to register Black residents.
He signed the 1799–1800 petition from Philadelphia's free Black community against the slave trade and the Fugitive Slave Act.

records.legacy: His granddaughter Charlotte Forten Grimké taught freedpeople during the Civil War; the 'Founding Black family' was the subject of a 2023 Museum of the American Revolution exhibition.

legacyDetail.d: His daughters Margaretta, Sarah and Harriet were founders of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society.

records.name: Richard Allen
records.scaleNote: Documented by his autobiography (1833), Mother Bethel records, the 1794 yellow fever narrative and AME founding minutes.
records.origins: Born enslaved in 1760 in the Philadelphia household of Benjamin Chew and sold with his family to Stokley Sturgis in Delaware. Converted by Methodists, he bought his freedom around 1780.
records.role_summary: With Absalom Jones he founded the Free African Society in 1787 and led Black worshippers out of St. George's Methodist Church after segregation. He opened Bethel church in 1794 on land he bought, which became Mother Bethel, and in 1816 led independent Black Methodist congregations to form the African Methodist Episcopal Church, serving as its first bishop.

roleDetail.d: Allen and Jones organised Black nurses and gravediggers during the epidemic and published a 1794 rebuttal to accusations of profiteering.
Mother Bethel sheltered freedom seekers; Allen also opposed the American Colonization Society.

records.legacy: Mother Bethel AME is described as the oldest property continuously owned by African Americans in the US; Allen's tomb is in its basement museum. The AME Church is now a global denomination with members on several continents.

legacyDetail.d: The St. George's walkout is traditionally dated 1787 but some historians place it in 1792–93.

sources.label: NPS — Preamble and Articles of Association of the Free African Society

records.name: Prince Hall
records.scaleNote: Documented by his 1770 manumission, the 1777 petition (Massachusetts Archives) and African Lodge records; early life details are uncertain.
records.origins: Enslaved in Boston by William Hall, a leather-dresser, he was freed in 1770. He worked as a leather worker and caterer.
records.role_summary: In 1775 he and 14 other free Black men were initiated into a British army Masonic lodge and formed African Lodge No. 1, later chartered by the Grand Lodge of England (warrant 1784, received 1787). In January 1777 he and seven others petitioned the Massachusetts legislature to abolish slavery, and in 1788 he protested the kidnapping of Black Bostonians into slavery.

roleDetail.d: His petitions used the language of natural rights against slavery and for Black schooling.
Several men named Prince Hall appear in records; whether he served is uncertain.

records.legacy: Prince Hall Freemasonry, with grand lodges across the US and abroad, is one of the oldest Black fraternal organisations. He is buried at Copp's Hill, Boston.

legacyDetail.d: Prince Hall grand lodges remain active civic organisations.

sources.label: National Constitution Center — Prince Hall petition to the Massachusetts Legislature (1777)

records.name: Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett)
records.scaleNote: Documented by Berkshire County court records of Brom and Bett v. Ashley (1781) and accounts by Catharine Sedgwick.
records.origins: Born enslaved around 1742–44 in New York, she was held by Colonel John Ashley in Sheffield, Massachusetts. Tradition says she was struck with a hot shovel by Ashley's wife.
records.role_summary: After hearing the new Massachusetts constitution of 1780 declare all men 'born free and equal', she sought out lawyer Theodore Sedgwick. In Brom and Bett v. Ashley the county court on 22 August 1781 ruled them free and awarded 30 shillings damages. She took the name Elizabeth Freeman and worked as a paid servant and well-known midwife.

roleDetail.d: With Quock Walker's cases (1781–83), her suit helped end slavery in Massachusetts by judicial interpretation.
A man named Brom, also enslaved by Ashley, joined the suit, perhaps because a woman's standing was weaker.

records.legacy: She is buried in the Sedgwick family plot in Stockbridge; a statue was unveiled in Sheffield in 2022. Her story is taught as a founding moment of Massachusetts abolition.

legacyDetail.d: A 1811 watercolour miniature by Susan Sedgwick is at the Massachusetts Historical Society.

sources.label: Mass Moments — Jury Decides in Favor of Elizabeth 'Mum Bett' Freeman
Massachusetts Women's History — Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett)

records.name: Solomon Northup
records.scaleNote: Documented by his 1853 narrative Twelve Years a Slave (verified by Sue Eakin's research), New York and DC court records of the kidnapping case.
records.base: Saratoga Springs, New York (enslaved at Bayou Boeuf, Louisiana)
records.origins: Born free in Minerva, New York, the son of a formerly enslaved man, he was a farmer, carpenter and violinist living with his wife and three children in Saratoga Springs.
records.role_summary: In 1841 two men lured him to Washington with offers of work, drugged him and sold him to slave trader James H. Birch, who held him in the Williams slave pen within sight of the Capitol. Shipped via Richmond to New Orleans and sold as 'Platt', he was enslaved for twelve years in Louisiana's Red River region, ten of them under the brutal Edwin Epps, until a Canadian carpenter carried letters north and New York's governor sent an agent who freed him on 3 January 1853.

roleDetail.d: Birch was tried in Washington in 1853 but acquitted; Black testimony was barred.
His sale shows the interstate trade from the Chesapeake to the Deep South at work.

records.legacy: Twelve Years a Slave sold about 30,000 copies in its first years and became an Oscar-winning film in 2013. Saratoga Springs holds an annual Solomon Northup Day; his date and place of death are unknown.

legacyDetail.d: Sue Eakin and Joseph Logsdon's 1968 annotated edition confirmed many details from Louisiana records.

sources.label: Learning for Justice — The Kidnapping Case (1853)

connections.label: shipped south like the 1838 Jesuit sale

records.name: Toussaint Louverture
records.scaleNote: Defining figure of the Haitian Revolution, documented by his letters, proclamations, the 1801 constitution and French colonial archives.
records.origins: Born enslaved around 1743 on the Bréda plantation near Cap-Français, he became a coachman and livestock steward and was freed by about 1776. Archival work shows that, as a free man, he leased a small coffee plantation worked by enslaved people.
records.role_summary: After the 1791 uprising in the northern plain he rose as a commander, first allied with Spain, then from 1794 with the French Republic after it abolished slavery. He defeated British and Spanish forces and rivals, and his 1801 constitution made him governor-general for life. Napoleon sent an expedition to restore control; Toussaint was seized during a parley in June 1802 and died imprisoned at Fort de Joux on 7 April 1803.

roleDetail.d: He kept plantation production going with compulsory labour for the formerly enslaved, a contested legacy.
Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haitian independence on 1 January 1804.

records.legacy: Haiti became the first state founded by formerly enslaved people, then paid France a crippling indemnity from 1825. Toussaint is honoured in Haiti, France (a plaque in the Panthéon, 1998) and across the Black Atlantic.

legacyDetail.d: Abolitionists and later anti-colonial writers, notably C. L. R. James (The Black Jacobins, 1938), made him an emblem of liberation.

sources.label: History Hit — 10 Facts About Toussaint Louverture

connections.label: born enslaved on the Bréda plantation
independent Haiti later forced to pay France
Haiti as refuge in Vesey's plot

records.name: Nanny of the Maroons
records.scaleNote: Few documents (British military reports, a 1740 land patent) survive; most of her story comes from Maroon oral tradition, so scale reflects impact more than records.
records.base: Nanny Town / Moore Town, Blue Mountains, Jamaica
records.origins: Oral tradition holds she was an Akan (often said Asante) woman, born in West Africa and brought to Jamaica enslaved, who escaped to the Blue Mountains.
records.role_summary: She led the Windward Maroons, who fought British forces for years during the First Maroon War from mountain strongholds including Nanny Town, which the British attacked in the 1730s. The Windward Maroons made peace in 1739–40 (Quao's treaty is variously dated June 1739 or April 1740), and a 1740 patent granted Nanny and her people 500 acres, where Moore Town stands.

roleDetail.d: Oral history credits her with obeah power and guerrilla tactics.
The treaties guaranteed Maroon freedom and land but required Maroons to return future runaways.

records.legacy: Jamaica designated her a National Hero in 1975 (the Order was conferred in 1976), the only woman so honoured; she appears on the $500 banknote. Moore Town's Maroon heritage is recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage (2008) and the Blue and John Crow Mountains are a World Heritage Site (2015).

legacyDetail.d: Moore Town Maroons maintain their own leadership and traditions.

sources.label: Royal Museums Greenwich — Nanny of the Maroons
Understanding Slavery Initiative — Nanny and the Maroons
Jamaica Gleaner — Nanny was real, not myth: Gov’t conferred Order of National Hero on Nanny in 1976

records.name: Zumbi dos Palmares
records.scaleNote: A defining figure of Brazilian Black resistance; documented through Portuguese colonial correspondence and expedition reports, though much of his biography is uncertain.
records.base: Serra da Barriga, Alagoas (then Pernambuco), Brazil
records.origins: Accounts say he was born free in Palmares around 1655, captured as a child by a Portuguese expedition and raised by a priest, then returned to Palmares as a teenager; this tradition rests on thin evidence.
records.role_summary: He rejected the 1678 peace treaty that his predecessor Ganga Zumba made with Pernambuco's governor, and led Palmares in continued war. In 1694 forces under the bandeirante Domingos Jorge Velho destroyed the capital, Macaco; Zumbi was betrayed and killed on 20 November 1695, and his head displayed in Recife.

roleDetail.d: Palmares was a confederation of quilombos holding thousands of people for most of the 17th century.
The story that he was raised by Father António Melo is widely repeated but weakly sourced.

records.legacy: 20 November is Brazil's Dia Nacional de Zumbi e da Consciência Negra, made a national holiday by Law 14.759 of December 2023. Serra da Barriga hosts the Parque Memorial Quilombo dos Palmares, and Zumbi is inscribed in the Book of Heroes of the Fatherland.

legacyDetail.d: The date was proposed in 1971 by Grupo Palmares in Porto Alegre as an alternative to 13 May abolition day.

sources.label: Agência Brasil — Zumbi dos Palmares: a 17th century leader's death is celebrated

connections.label: Black Consciousness Day chosen over 13 May abolition

records.name: Underground Railroad
records.description: A loose network of routes, safe houses and people — mostly free and enslaved African Americans, with white and Quaker allies — that helped freedom seekers escape slavery to the free states, Canada, Mexico and elsewhere, especially from the 1830s to 1865. Maryland's Eastern Shore and Baltimore were major points of departure. The NPS Network to Freedom programme (1998) now recognises hundreds of documented sites.

connections.label: escape route by rail and ship

records.name: African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church and Mother Bethel
records.description: Richard Allen opened Bethel church in Philadelphia in 1794 on land he bought; it is the 'Mother Bethel' of the AME Church, founded in 1816 when Black Methodist congregations from Philadelphia, Baltimore and elsewhere united as the first independent Black denomination in the US. Charleston's AME congregation, linked to Denmark Vesey, was suppressed in 1822 and refounded as Mother Emanuel. The church remains a major international denomination.

connections.label: grew out of the Free African Society

records.name: Free African Society (Philadelphia) and St. Thomas's African Episcopal Church
records.description: Founded in April 1787 by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones (1746–1818) as a mutual aid society for Philadelphia's free Black community. Jones, born enslaved in Delaware and self-purchased in 1784, led the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas (opened 1794), was ordained the first Black Episcopal priest in 1802, led the 1799–1800 petition to Congress against the slave trade, and preached a Thanksgiving sermon on 1 January 1808 when the US ban on the slave trade took effect.

records.name: Freedom's Journal (1827–1829)
records.description: The first African American-owned and -edited newspaper in the US, launched in New York on 16 March 1827 by Samuel Cornish and John Russwurm ('We wish to plead our own cause'). It had agents across the North, the upper South, Canada, Britain and Haiti. After Russwurm turned to colonisation and left for Liberia in 1829, Cornish relaunched it as The Rights of All.

connections.label: Philadelphia supporter of the Black press

records.name: Quilombo dos Palmares
records.description: The largest and longest-lasting maroon community in the Americas, formed by people escaping sugar plantations in Pernambuco from about 1600 and holding thousands of inhabitants in the Serra da Barriga region. It resisted Dutch (1640s) and Portuguese expeditions for most of the century, under leaders including Ganga Zumba and Zumbi, until its destruction in 1694–95. Serra da Barriga is now a national memorial park.

records.name: Malê Revolt, Salvador (1835)
records.description: On the night of 24–25 January 1835, during Ramadan, some 600 enslaved and freed Africans, led by Muslims (malês) mostly of Yoruba (Nagô) and Hausa origin, rose in Salvador da Bahia and fought troops in the streets before being defeated. Per historian João José Reis, dozens of rebels died; four men were executed by firing squad on 14 May 1835, and hundreds were flogged, imprisoned or deported to Africa. Luísa Mahin, celebrated as a leader and mother of abolitionist Luiz Gama, is known only from her son's writings, and historians question her role.

connections.label: Oyo's collapse sent many Yoruba captives to Bahia
deportees joined returnee communities in Benin and Lagos

records.name: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park and State Park
records.description: Proclaimed a national monument in 2013 and a national historical park in 2014, the 480-acre park in Dorchester County, Maryland, preserves landscapes of Tubman's early life, including Joseph Stewart's Canal, dug by enslaved and free Black workers. A Maryland state park visitor centre opened in 2017; the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway links sites across the Eastern Shore.

records.name: Frederick Douglass National Historic Site (Cedar Hill)
records.description: Douglass's home in Anacostia, Washington DC, from 1877 until his death in 1895. Helen Pitts Douglass and the National Association of Colored Women preserved it, and it became an NPS site in 1962.

records.name: Point Comfort / Fort Monroe National Monument and 1619 African Landing Memorial
records.description: Point Comfort, where the White Lion landed '20 and odd' Africans in August 1619, later became Fort Monroe, where three self-emancipated men sought Union protection in 1861 and were declared 'contraband of war'. Fort Monroe became a National Monument in 2011, and an African Landing Memorial is under development.

records.name: GU272 Descendants Association and Georgetown descendant programmes
records.description: Descendants of the 272 people sold by the Maryland Jesuits in 1838 organised after the 2016 revelations, pressing Georgetown and the Jesuits for reparative action. Outcomes include Georgetown's 2017 apology and admissions preference, the 2019 student-backed Reconciliation Fund, and the Jesuits' 2021 $100m pledge to the Descendants Truth & Reconciliation Foundation.

events.title: '20 and odd' Africans reach Point Comfort
events.text: English privateers trade Ndongo captives seized from the Portuguese São João Bautista for food at Point Comfort, Virginia; Angela arrives days later on the Treasurer.

source.label: NPS — Arrival of the First Africans in 1619

events.title: Zumbi killed; Palmares falls
events.text: After the 1694 destruction of Macaco, Zumbi is betrayed and killed on 20 November 1695.

events.title: Windward Maroons make peace
events.text: Nanny's Windward Maroons make peace with the British and receive a 500-acre land grant, later Moore Town.

source.label: Royal Museums Greenwich — Nanny of the Maroons

events.title: Brom and Bett v. Ashley
events.text: A Berkshire County jury frees Elizabeth Freeman and Brom under the 1780 Massachusetts constitution.

source.label: Mass Moments — Jury Decides in Favor of Elizabeth Freeman

events.title: Free African Society founded
events.text: Richard Allen and Absalom Jones found a mutual aid society in Philadelphia, root of Mother Bethel and St. Thomas's.

events.title: Banneker writes to Jefferson; Saint-Domingue rises
events.text: In August Benjamin Banneker challenges Jefferson on slavery; days later enslaved people rise in northern Saint-Domingue, the start of the revolution Toussaint Louverture would lead.

source.label: Founders Online — Banneker to Jefferson, 19 August 1791

events.title: Ona Judge escapes the President's House
events.text: On 21 May Ona Judge flees the Washingtons in Philadelphia and reaches Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

events.title: Gabriel's Conspiracy
events.text: A planned rising near Richmond is delayed by a storm and betrayed; Gabriel and 25 others are hanged.

events.title: AME Church founded
events.text: Black Methodists from Philadelphia, Baltimore and elsewhere found the African Methodist Episcopal Church; Richard Allen becomes bishop after Daniel Coker steps aside.

events.title: Denmark Vesey plot crushed in Charleston
events.text: Scores of Black Charlestonians are arrested; 35, including Vesey, are hanged and the AME church destroyed.

events.title: Nat Turner's revolt
events.text: Turner's revolt in Southampton County kills about 55 white people; brutal reprisals and new restrictive laws follow.

events.title: Malê Revolt in Salvador
events.text: African Muslims lead an urban uprising in Salvador da Bahia, followed by executions, floggings and deportations.

events.title: Maryland Jesuits sell 272 people
events.text: The Jesuits sell 272 enslaved people from their Maryland plantations to Louisiana planters for about $115,000, partly to pay Georgetown's debts.

events.title: Frederick Douglass escapes Baltimore
events.text: On 3 September Douglass leaves Baltimore by train, disguised as a sailor, and reaches New York within a day.

events.title: Harriet Tubman escapes Dorchester County
events.text: Tubman escapes to Philadelphia and soon begins returning to Maryland to lead family members and others north.

source.label: Maryland State Archives — Harriet Ross Tubman Davis

events.title: Georgetown 272 descendants come forward
events.text: Reporting and the Georgetown Memory Project trace living descendants of the 1838 sale, leading to Georgetown's 2017 apology and later a $100m Jesuit pledge (2021).
